standing_assumptions: Setting. The work is a textbook: Aronow and Miller, Foundations of Agnostic Statistics (Cambridge University Press, 2019). Every statement is about random variables on a probability space; Part II adds i.i.d. sampling; Part III adds the missing-data and potential-outcomes models. Locations give the printed page and the one-based page of main.pdf (316 pp.; in the body, PDF page = printed page + 18). Statements were transcribed from the page images (the 110 dpi staged renders, with higher-resolution renders of the same PDF pages where subscripts were small) and compared with the text layer for wording. (S1) Probability space. [Definition 1.1.1, p. 6 (PDF p. 24)] A set $S$ of subsets of $\Omega$ is an event space if it satisfies the following: Nonempty: $S \ne \emptyset$. Closed under complements: if $A \in S$, then $A^C \in S$. Closed under countable unions: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$, then $A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ... \in S$. [Definition 1.1.2, p. 7 (PDF p. 25)] Kolmogorov Axioms. Let $\Omega$ be a sample space, $S$ be an event space, and $P$ be a probability measure. Then $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space if it satisfies the following: Non-negativity: $\forall A \in S$, $P(A) \ge 0$, where $P(A)$ is finite and real. Unitarity: $P(\Omega) = 1$. Countable additivity: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$ are pairwise disjoint, then $P(A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ...) = P(A_1) + P(A_2) + P(A_3) + ... = \sum_i P(A_i)$. [Footnote 11, p. 8 (PDF p. 26)] This assumption [that $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space] shall henceforth be implicit in all definitions and theorems referring to $\Omega$, $S$, and/or $P$. (S2) Random variables and their distributions. [Definition 1.2.1, p. 16 (PDF p. 34)] A random variable is a function $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ such that, $\forall r \in \mathbb{R}$, $\{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) \le r\} \in S$. [Definition 1.2.2, p. 16] Let $g : U \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function, where $X(\Omega) \subseteq U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Then, if $g \circ X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ is a random variable, we say that $g$ is a function of $X$, and write $g(X)$ to denote the random variable $g \circ X$. [p. 17 (PDF p. 35)] we use $\Pr[\cdot]$ to denote the probability that some condition(s) on a random variable will hold, or, equivalently, the probability that the event defined by those conditions will occur. [Definition 1.2.4, p. 18 (PDF p. 36)] A random variable $X$ is discrete if its range, $X(\Omega)$, is a countable set. [Definition 1.2.5, p. 18] For a discrete random variable $X$, the probability mass function of $X$ is $f(x) = \Pr[X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.11, p. 21 (PDF p. 39)] For a random variable $X$, the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.14, p. 24 (PDF p. 42)] A random variable $X$ is continuous if there exists a non-negative function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that the CDF of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x] = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f(u)du$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. The function $f$ is called the probability density function (PDF). [Definition 1.2.15, p. 25 (PDF p. 43), as printed; see finding P001-C01-E002] For a continuous random variable $X$ with CDF $F$, the probability density function of $X$ is $f(x) = \left.\frac{dF(u)}{du}\right|_{u=x}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.20, p. 31 (PDF p. 49)] For a random variable $X$ with PMF/PDF $f$, the support of $X$ is $\mathrm{Supp}[X] = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : f(x) > 0\}$. [Definition 1.3.1, p. 31] Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. Then $X = Y$ if, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $X(\omega) = Y(\omega)$. [Definition 1.3.16, p. 38 (PDF p. 56)] Let $X$ and $Y$ be either two discrete random variables with joint PMF $f$ or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF $f$. Then $X$ and $Y$ are independent if, $\forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}$, $f(x, y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y)$. We write $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y$. [Definition 1.4.1, p. 39 (PDF p. 57)] A random vector (of length $K$) is a function $\mathbf{X} : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^K$ such that, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $\mathbf{X}(\omega) = (X_{[1]}(\omega), X_{[2]}(\omega), ..., X_{[K]}(\omega))$, where $\forall k \in \{1, 2, ..., K\}$, $X_{[k]}$ is a random variable. (S3) Expectations. [Definition 2.1.1, p. 45 (PDF p. 63)] For a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function (PMF) $f$, if $\sum_x |x|f(x) < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \sum_x xf(x)$. For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function (PDF) $f$, if $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |x|f(x)dx < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} xf(x)dx$. [Footnote 2, p. 45] This regularity condition (and the corresponding one in the continuous case) is known as absolute convergence. It is virtually always satisfied in practice, so we omit this technical condition from all subsequent discussion of expectations. [Footnote 3, p. 49 (PDF p. 67)] This theorem, and every subsequent theorem that we only prove for these two cases [two discrete random variables with joint PMF, or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF], also holds when one random variable is discrete and the other continuous. [Definition 2.1.12, p. 52 (PDF p. 70)] The variance of a random variable $X$ is $\mathrm{V}[X] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])^2]$. [Definition 2.1.15, p. 53 (PDF p. 71)] The standard deviation of a random variable $X$ is $\sigma[X] = \sqrt{\mathrm{V}[X]}$. [Definition 2.1.22, p. 57 (PDF p. 75)] For a random variable $X$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, the mean squared error of $X$ about $c$ is $\mathrm{E}[(X - c)^2]$. [Definition 2.2.1, p. 59 (PDF p. 77)] The covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is $\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y])]$. [Definition 2.2.5, p. 62 (PDF p. 80)] The correlation of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ with $\sigma[X] > 0$ and $\sigma[Y] > 0$ is $\rho[X, Y] = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y]}{\sigma[X]\sigma[Y]}$. [Definition 2.2.10, p. 67 (PDF p. 85)] For discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \sum_y yf_{Y|X}(y|x)$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. For jointly continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PDF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} yf_{Y|X}(y|x)dy$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.12, p. 68 (PDF p. 86)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$, the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{V}[Y|X = x] = \mathrm{E}[(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x])^2|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.15, p. 69 (PDF p. 87)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF/PDF $f$, the conditional expectation function of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $G_Y(x) = \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [p. 70 (PDF p. 88)] We write $\mathrm{E}[Y|X]$ to denote $G_Y(X)$; the conditional variance function is $H_Y(x) = \mathrm{V}[Y|X = x]$, and $\mathrm{V}[Y|X]$ denotes the random variable $H_Y(X)$. [Footnote 14, p. 70] Ignoring some unimportant measure-theoretic regularity conditions, namely $X(\Omega) = \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. The multivariate versions are Definitions 2.3.3 and 2.3.4 (p. 85, PDF p. 103) and the multivariate BLP, Definition 2.3.6 (p. 86, PDF p. 104; transcribed in the targets that use it). (S4) Sampling and asymptotics. [Definition 3.1.1, p. 92 (PDF p. 110)] Let $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ be random variables with CDFs $F_1, F_2, ..., F_n$, respectively. Let $F_A$ denote the joint CDF of the random variables with indices in the set $A$. Then $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ are independent and identically distributed if they satisfy the following: Mutually independent: $\forall A \subseteq \{1, 2, ..., n\}$, $\forall(x_1, x_2, ..., x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $F_A((x_i)_{i \in A}) = \prod_{i \in A} F_i(x_i)$. Identically distributed: $\forall i, j \in \{1, 2, ..., n\}$ and $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$, $F_i(x) = F_j(x)$. [p. 92] When we have i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, we use the unsubscripted letter $X$ to denote the random variable whose distribution the i.i.d. draws all share. So, for example, $\mathrm{E}[X]$ denotes the expected value common to $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, that is, $\mathrm{E}[X] = \mathrm{E}[X_1] = \mathrm{E}[X_2] = ... = \mathrm{E}[X_n]$. [Definition 3.2.1, p. 96 (PDF p. 114)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, a sample statistic is a function of $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$: $T_{(n)} = h_{(n)}(X_1, X_2, ..., X_n)$, where $h_{(n)} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, $\forall n \in \mathbb{N}$. [Definition 3.2.2, p. 97 (PDF p. 115)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the sample mean is $\overline{X} = \frac{X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_n}{n} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i$. [Definition 3.2.6, p. 99 (PDF p. 117)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables and let $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in probability to $c$ if, $\forall\epsilon > 0$, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| \ge \epsilon] = 0$, or equivalently, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| < \epsilon] = 1$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{p} c$. [Definition 3.2.22, p. 108 (PDF p. 126)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables with CDFs $(F_{(1)}, F_{(2)}, F_{(3)}, ...)$, and let $T$ be a random variable with CDF $F$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in distribution to $T$ if, $\forall t \in \mathbb{R}$ at which $F$ is continuous, $\lim_{n \to \infty} F_{(n)}(t) = F(t)$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{d} T$. [Definition 3.2.28, p. 112 (PDF p. 130)] An estimator $\hat\theta$ is asymptotically normal if $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \phi^2)$, for some finite $\phi > 0$. [Definition 3.3.1, p. 116 (PDF p. 134)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the empirical CDF $\hat F$ of $X$ is $\hat F(x) = \overline{\mathrm{I}(X \le x)}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 3.3.2, p. 118 (PDF p. 136)] A statistical functional is a function $T : \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is the set of all possible CDFs. [Definition 3.3.3, p. 118] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ with common CDF $F$, the plug-in estimator of $\theta = T(F)$ is $\hat\theta = T(\hat F)$. The 'usual plug-in regularity conditions' (p. 120, PDF p. 138) are not formally defined in the book (footnote 31 names Hadamard differentiability with respect to the Kolmogorov distance and gives no formal definition). (S5) Regression. [Definition 4.1.2, pp. 146–147 (PDF pp. 164–165), with the plus sign before the last term supplied] For i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$, the ordinary least squares (OLS) regression estimator is the function $\hat g(\mathbf{X}) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1X_{[1]} + \hat\beta_2X_{[2]} + ... + \hat\beta_KX_{[K]}$ such that $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1, ..., \hat\beta_K) = \arg\min_{(b_0, b_1, ..., b_K) \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_i - (b_0 + b_1X_{[1]i} + b_2X_{[2]i} + ... + b_KX_{[K]i})\right)^2$. We refer to $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ as the OLS coefficient estimator. [Definition 4.1.3, p. 148 (PDF p. 166)] the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ is the $n \times (K + 1)$ matrix whose $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ row is $(1, X_{[1]i}, X_{[2]i}, \cdots, X_{[K]i})$. (S6) Parametric models. [Definition 5.1.1, pp. 178–179 (PDF pp. 196–197)] For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X}$ of length $K$, a parametric model is a set of functions $g : \mathbb{R}^{K+1} \to \mathbb{R}$ indexed by a real-valued parameter vector $\boldsymbol\theta$ of length $\tau$: $\{g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta) : \boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta\}$, where $\boldsymbol\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^\tau$. The set $\boldsymbol\Theta$ is called the parameter space. The model is said to be true if $\exists\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$ such that $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. [Definition 5.2.1, p. 186 (PDF p. 204)] the likelihood function is $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y, \mathbf{X}) = g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})$, and for i.i.d. observations $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. [Definition 5.2.2, pp. 186–187 (PDF pp. 204–205)] the maximum likelihood estimator of $\boldsymbol\theta$ is $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. (S7) Missing data. [Definition 6.1.1, pp. 208–209 (PDF pp. 226–227)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$, the stable outcomes model is $Y_i^* = -99$ if $R_i = 0$ and $Y_i$ if $R_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, where $Y_i^*$ is the censored version of $Y_i$ and $R_i$ is an indicator for whether $Y_i$ is observed for unit $i$. [Footnote 2, p. 208] Since we are assuming i.i.d. sampling, our inferences do not depend on the unit subscript $i$. [Definition 6.1.5, p. 213 (PDF p. 231)] $Y_i$ is missing completely at random if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i$ and $\Pr[R_i = 1] > 0$. [Definition 6.1.8, p. 215 (PDF p. 233)] $Y_i$ is missing at random conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] > \epsilon$. [Footnote 6, p. 215] For random variables $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ with joint PMF/PDF $f(x, y, z)$, $Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z|X$ if, $\forall y, z \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$, $f_{(Y,Z)|X}((y, z)|x) = f_{Y|X}(y|x)f_{Z|X}(z|x)$. [Definition 6.1.11, p. 217 (PDF p. 235)] the response propensity function is $p_R(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. (S8) Causal inference. [Definition 7.1.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 254)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$ and binary treatment variable $D_i$, the potential outcomes model is $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$, where $Y_i(0)$ denotes the potential outcome under control for unit $i$, and $Y_i(1)$ denotes the potential outcome under treatment for unit $i$. [Definition 7.1.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 255)] $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. [Definition 7.1.3, p. 238 (PDF p. 256)] the average treatment effect (ATE) is $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$. [Definition 7.1.9, p. 244 (PDF p. 262)] $D_i$ is randomly assigned if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i$ and $0 < \Pr[D_i = 1] < 1$. [Definition 7.1.12, p. 247 (PDF p. 265)] $D_i$ is strongly ignorable conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\epsilon < \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] < 1 - \epsilon$. [Definition 7.1.15, p. 250 (PDF p. 268)] the treatment propensity function is $p_D(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. Notes for the formalizer. (a) The book works with PMFs and PDFs and states pointwise conditions ('for all $x$'); for continuous variables these hold only up to null sets (finding P001-C01-E002), so a measure-theoretic formalization should read densities and conditional expectations as versions. (b) Existence and finiteness of the expectations in a statement is a standing convention (footnote 2, p. 45). (c) Asymptotic statements are about an infinite i.i.d. sequence and $n \to \infty$. (d) In a target's statement, text in square brackets is a label or a remark of the transcriber, not the book's words.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Definition 4.3.9 (Polynomial Least Squares Sieve Estimator) and the consistency claim after it, corrected with a sufficient degree-growth condition
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected definition] Definition 4.3.9. Polynomial Least Squares Sieve Estimator. For i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, X_1), (Y_2, X_2), ..., (Y_n, X_n)$, the polynomial least squares sieve estimator of the conditional expectation function is $\hat{\mathrm{E}}_n[Y|X = x] = \sum_{k=0}^{J_n}\hat\beta_kx^k$, where $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{J_n+1}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_i - \sum_{k=0}^{J_n} b_kX_i^k\right)^2$, where $J_n \to \infty$ and the degree grows slowly enough that the sample fit is stable in a population-normalized polynomial basis and the sampling noise vanishes. [One explicit sufficient version, with every hypothesis] Let $(Y_i, X_i)$ be i.i.d., let $\mathrm{Supp}[X] = [a, b]$ be a compact interval, let $m(x) = \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x]$ be continuous on $[a, b]$, and let $\mathrm{Var}(Y|X) \le V < \infty$. Let $p_0, ..., p_{J_n}$ be polynomials with $\deg p_k = k$ that are orthonormal in $L^2(P_X)$, that is, $\mathrm{E}[p_j(X)p_k(X)] = \mathbb{1}\{j = k\}$, let $P$ be the $n \times (J_n + 1)$ matrix with entries $p_k(X_i)$ and $G_n = P^TP/n$. If $J_n \to \infty$, $(J_n + 1)/n \to 0$, and for some fixed $c > 0$, $\Pr[\lambda_{\min}(G_n) \ge c] \to 1$, then $\int(\hat m_n(x) - m(x))^2dP_X(x) \xrightarrow{p} 0$, where $\hat m_n(x) = \hat{\mathrm{E}}_n[Y|X = x]$. The Gram condition holds if $\zeta_K^2K/n \to 0$ with $K = J_n + 1$ and $\zeta_K^2 = \sup_x\sum_{k=0}^{J_n} p_k(x)^2$. [Uniform covariates] If $X$ is uniform on a compact interval, $\zeta_K^2 \le K^2$, and $(J_n + 1)^3/n \to 0$ suffices: $\Pr\left[\|G_n - I\|_{\mathrm{op}} > \frac{1}{2}\right] \le \frac{4((J_n + 1)^3 - (J_n + 1))}{n}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$; the multivariate BLP (Definition 2.3.6); the CEF (Definition 2.2.15) and its domain $\mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}]$; expected value, variance and covariance; convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); the OLS regression estimator (Definition 4.1.2) and the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ (Definition 4.1.3). [Theorem 4.3.2, p. 158 (PDF p. 176)] Weierstrass Approximation Theorem. Let $f : [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous. Then, $\forall \epsilon > 0$, there exists a polynomial $p$ such that $\forall x \in [a, b]$, $|f(x) - p(x)| < \epsilon$. [Notation of the validators] $P_X$ the distribution of $X$; $\lambda_{\min}$ the smallest eigenvalue; $\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ the operator norm; $L_k$ the Legendre polynomials, with $p_k(x) = \sqrt{2k + 1}L_k(2x - 1)$ orthonormal for $X \sim U(0, 1)$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: [Exact steps of the repair proof, validators' derivation, Section 8, for each $n$] For $\epsilon > 0$ let $h$ be a polynomial with $\sup_x|m(x) - h(x)| \le \epsilon$ (Weierstrass), of degree at most $J_n$ for large $n$, with basis coefficients $b_h$. Then $\hat b = b_h + b_r + b_u$ with $b_r = (P^TP)^{-1}P^Tr$, $b_u = (P^TP)^{-1}P^Tu$, $r_i = m(X_i) - h(X_i)$, $u_i = Y_i - m(X_i)$. On $\{\lambda_{\min}(G_n) \ge c\}$: $c\|b_r\|^2 \le b_r^TG_nb_r \le \|r\|^2/n \le \epsilon^2$ and $\mathrm{E}[\|b_u\|^2|X_1, ..., X_n] \le V\mathrm{tr}(G_n^{-1})/n \le V(J_n + 1)/(cn)$; and $\|\hat m_n - m\|_{L^2(P_X)} \le \epsilon(1 + c^{-1/2}) + \|b_u\|$. For the uniform design: $\mathrm{E}\|G_n - I_q\|_F^2 = \frac{\mathrm{E}[K_J(X)^2] - q}{n} \le \frac{q^3 - q}{n}$ with $q = J + 1$ and $K_J(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{J} p_k(x)^2 \le q^2$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Moderate. The repair keeps the same estimator, estimand and conclusion and replaces the false sufficient rate by a stronger one; no optimality is claimed, and the cubic rate is specific to uniform covariates. The qualitative claim (slow enough growth gives consistency) survives. Headline claim P001-ch04-H8 holds with the corrected rate. The squared residual is restored here (finding P001-C04-E003).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Theorem 5.2.8 (The ML Estimator Is Consistent for the Minimum KL Divergence Predictor), with the target defined by the KL divergence at a fixed $\mathbf{x}$, as printed
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] Theorem 5.2.8. The ML Estimator Is Consistent for the Minimum KL Divergence Predictor. Let $Y$ be a random variable and $\mathbf{X}$ be a random vector. Let $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$ be i.i.d. observations of $(Y, \mathbf{X})$. Then the ML estimate of $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x})$, $g(y, \mathbf{x}; \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML})$ consistently estimates the minimum Kullback–Leibler divergence approximation of $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x})$ among all probability distributions of the form $g(y, \mathbf{x}; \mathbf{t})$. That is, assuming that there exists a unique $\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathrm{KL}\left[f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(\cdot|\mathbf{x})\,\|\,g(\cdot, \mathbf{x}; \mathbf{t})\right]$, then $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} \xrightarrow{p} \tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}$. [What is refuted] The displayed target: the minimizer of the KL divergence at a fixed value $\mathbf{x}$, with no expectation over the distribution of $\mathbf{X}$. The intended result, with the KL divergence averaged over $\mathbf{X}$, is not refuted. [Counterexample, from the validators] Let $(X, Y)$ have joint PMF $\Pr[X = 0, Y = 0] = \frac{3}{8}$, $\Pr[X = 0, Y = 1] = \frac{1}{8}$, $\Pr[X = 1, Y = 0] = \frac{1}{8}$, $\Pr[X = 1, Y = 1] = \frac{3}{8}$, so that $\Pr[X = 1] = \frac{1}{2}$, $\Pr[Y = 1|X = 0] = \frac{1}{4}$ and $\Pr[Y = 1|X = 1] = \frac{3}{4}$. Let the model be $g(y, x; t) = t^y(1 - t)^{1-y}$ for $y \in \{0, 1\}$, with $\boldsymbol\Theta = [\frac{1}{10}, \frac{9}{10}]$. Then: (a) for a true conditional success probability $p$, $K_p(t) = \mathrm{KL}[f_{Y|X}(\cdot|x)\,\|\,g(\cdot, x; t)] = p\log\frac{p}{t} + (1 - p)\log\frac{1 - p}{1 - t}$ has $K_p'(t) = \frac{t - p}{t(1 - t)}$, so the printed target is unique at each $x$: $\arg\min_{t \in \boldsymbol\Theta} K_{1/4}(t) = \frac{1}{4}$ at $x = 0$ and $\arg\min_{t \in \boldsymbol\Theta} K_{3/4}(t) = \frac{3}{4}$ at $x = 1$; (b) for every sample the ML estimator exists, is unique and equals $\hat t_n = \mathrm{clip}_{[1/10, 9/10]}(\overline{Y})$; (c) $\mathrm{E}[Y] = \frac{1}{2}$, $\mathrm{V}[Y] = \frac{1}{4}$, and for every $\epsilon > 0$, $\Pr[|\hat t_n - \frac{1}{2}| \ge \epsilon] \le \frac{1}{4n\epsilon^2}$, so $\hat t_n \xrightarrow{p} \frac{1}{2}$; (d) with $\epsilon = \frac{1}{8}$: $\Pr[|\hat t_n - \frac{1}{4}| > \frac{1}{8}] \ge 1 - \frac{16}{n}$ and $\Pr[|\hat t_n - \frac{3}{4}| > \frac{1}{8}] \ge 1 - \frac{16}{n}$, so $\hat t_n$ converges in probability to neither printed target; (e) the averaged divergence $D(t) = \frac{1}{2}K_{1/4}(t) + \frac{1}{2}K_{3/4}(t)$ has $D'(t) = \frac{t - 1/2}{t(1 - t)}$ and unique minimizer $\frac{1}{2}$, with $D(\frac{1}{4}) - D(\frac{1}{2}) = D(\frac{3}{4}) - D(\frac{1}{2}) = \frac{1}{2}\log\frac{4}{3} > 0$; (f) if $\Pr[X = 1] = q$ with the conditional laws unchanged, the limit of the ML estimator is $\frac{1}{4} + \frac{q}{2}$ (for example $\frac{3}{8}$ at $q = \frac{1}{4}$).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: parametric model and its truth (Definition 5.1.1); likelihood function (Definition 5.2.1); maximum likelihood estimator (Definition 5.2.2); the CEF (Definitions 2.2.15, 2.3.4); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); i.i.d. observations $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$ of $(Y, \mathbf{X})$. [Definition 5.2.1, p. 186 (PDF p. 204)] Likelihood Function. Let $Y$ be a random variable and $\mathbf{X}$ be a random vector, and assume the parametric model $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. Then the likelihood function is $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y, \mathbf{X}) = g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})$. For i.i.d. observations, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. [Definition 5.2.2, pp. 186–187 (PDF pp. 204–205)] Maximum Likelihood Estimator. For the parametric model $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$ with $\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$, the maximum likelihood estimator of $\boldsymbol\theta$ is $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, or, equivalently, $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}[\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X})] = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, where $\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X})$ is known as the log-likelihood. [Definition 5.2.7, p. 195] Kullback–Leibler Divergence for Continuous Distributions. For probability density functions $p(\cdot)$ and $q(\cdot)$, the Kullback–Leibler divergence is $\mathrm{KL}[p(\cdot)\,\|\,q(\cdot)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} p(t)\log\left(\frac{p(t)}{q(t)}\right)dt$. The KL divergence is defined analogously for discrete random variables, with a sum replacing the integral and PMFs replacing PDFs.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact for each $n$: the likelihood is $t^{N_1}(1 - t)^{n - N_1}$ with $N_1 = \sum_i Y_i$, and $L_n(t) = a\log t + (1 - a)\log(1 - t)$ with $a = N_1/n$ has $L_n'(t) = \frac{a - t}{t(1 - t)}$, so the unique maximizer on $[\frac{1}{10}, \frac{9}{10}]$ is the clipped $a$; $\mathrm{V}[a] = \frac{1}{4n}$; clipping onto an interval containing $\frac{1}{2}$ does not increase the distance from $\frac{1}{2}$; Chebyshev's inequality gives the bounds in (c) and (d). Also $\sup_{t \in \boldsymbol\Theta}|L_n(t) - M(t)| \le |a - \frac{1}{2}|\log 9$ with $M(t) = \frac{1}{2}\log t + \frac{1}{2}\log(1 - t)$, so the example satisfies uniform convergence, compactness, continuity and uniqueness.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Moderate (dual validation; confirmed in part: the missing expectation is a defect of the formal display, while the prose on pp. 194 and 196 carries the averaged target). The model ignores the covariate, which the theorem permits. The counterexample has every regularity property usually required, so the failure is not due to omitted regularity conditions.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Theorem 5.2.8 (The ML Estimator Is Consistent for the Minimum KL Divergence Predictor), corrected: the KL divergence averaged over the distribution of $\mathbf{X}$
canonical_claim.location: p. 195 (PDF p. 213), Theorem 5.2.8; the explanatory paragraphs on p. 196 (PDF p. 214)
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected statement] Theorem 5.2.8. Let $Y$ be a random variable and $\mathbf{X}$ be a random vector. Let $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$ be i.i.d. observations of $(Y, \mathbf{X})$. Then, under the requisite regularity conditions for ML consistency (as in Theorem 5.2.6), assuming that there exists a unique $\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathrm{E}_{\mathbf{X}}\left[\mathrm{KL}\left\{f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(\cdot|\mathbf{X})\,\|\,g(\cdot, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})\right\}\right]$, then $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} \xrightarrow{p} \tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}$. (When the averaged KL divergence is not finite, define $\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}$ as the maximizer of $\mathrm{E}[\log g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})]$.) On p. 196, 'closest (in terms of KL divergence)' and 'the KL divergence of the hypothesized distribution from the true population distribution' mean the divergence averaged over the covariate distribution. [Formal content] (i) Identity: if $C = \mathrm{E}_{\mathbf{X}}\left[\int f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{X})\log f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{X})dy\right]$ and $M(\mathbf{t}) = \mathrm{E}[\log g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})]$ are finite, then $D(\mathbf{t}) := \mathrm{E}_{\mathbf{X}}\left[\mathrm{KL}\{f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(\cdot|\mathbf{X})\,\|\,g(\cdot, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})\}\right] = C - M(\mathbf{t})$, so minimizing $D$ over $\boldsymbol\Theta$ is the same as maximizing $M$ (sums replace integrals for PMFs). (ii) Consistency: let $L_n(\mathbf{t}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log g(Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i; \mathbf{t})$ and suppose (1) $\Delta_n = \sup_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}|L_n(\mathbf{t}) - M(\mathbf{t})| \xrightarrow{p} 0$; (2) there is $\mathbf{t}_* \in \boldsymbol\Theta$ such that for every $\epsilon > 0$, $\delta_\epsilon = M(\mathbf{t}_*) - \sup_{\|\mathbf{t} - \mathbf{t}_*\| \ge \epsilon} M(\mathbf{t}) > 0$; (3) $L_n(\hat{\mathbf{t}}_n) \ge \sup_{\mathbf{t}} L_n(\mathbf{t}) - e_n$ with $e_n \ge 0$, $e_n \xrightarrow{p} 0$. Then $\hat{\mathbf{t}}_n \xrightarrow{p} \mathbf{t}_*$. Compactness of $\boldsymbol\Theta$, continuity of $M$ and a unique maximizer imply (2). (iii) If the model is true at $\boldsymbol\theta$, then $D(\boldsymbol\theta) = 0$ and $\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta} = \boldsymbol\theta$ (p. 196).

canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: [Exact steps of the consistency argument, validators' derivation] On the event $2\Delta_n + e_n < \delta_\epsilon$: $M(\hat{\mathbf{t}}_n) \ge L_n(\hat{\mathbf{t}}_n) - \Delta_n \ge L_n(\mathbf{t}_*) - e_n - \Delta_n \ge M(\mathbf{t}_*) - 2\Delta_n - e_n > M(\mathbf{t}_*) - \delta_\epsilon$, which forces $\|\hat{\mathbf{t}}_n - \mathbf{t}_*\| < \epsilon$. The identity (i) is the expansion $\log\frac{f}{g} = \log f - \log g$ followed by the Law of Iterated Expectations.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Moderate. The repair changes the estimand named in the display (from a fixed-$\mathbf{x}$ minimizer to the minimizer of the population-averaged divergence) and leaves every method, example and figure unchanged; it gives no guarantee of minimum KL divergence separately at each $\mathbf{x}$. Headline claim P001-ch05-H5 (ML consistently estimates the member of the family with minimum KL divergence from the true conditional distribution) holds in this averaged sense. The book omits the proof of Theorem 5.2.8.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 5.2.5 and Example 5.2.11: 'the product can be maximized to find the ML estimate', applied to the normal/log-normal/exponential mixture, as printed
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statements] [pp. 198–199] Suppose that the distribution of $Y$ conditional on $\mathbf{X}$ can be represented as a weighted average of $M$ different parametric models, $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta) = p_1g_1(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta_1) + p_2g_2(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta_2) + ... + \left(1 - \sum_{m=1}^{M-1} p_m\right)g_M(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta_M)$, where $\boldsymbol\theta = (p_1, \boldsymbol\theta_1, p_2, \boldsymbol\theta_2, ..., p_{M-1}, \boldsymbol\theta_{M-1}, \boldsymbol\theta_M)$. Then, as before, $\prod_{i=1}^{n} g(Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i; \boldsymbol\theta)$ can be maximized to find the ML estimate of $\boldsymbol\theta$. (This can sometimes be computationally tricky.) [Example 5.2.11, pp. 199–200] $g_N(y; (\mu_N, \sigma_N)) = \frac{1}{\sigma_N\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{(y - \mu_N)^2}{2\sigma_N^2}}$; $g_{LN}(y; (\mu_{LN}, \sigma_{LN})) = \frac{1}{y\sigma_{LN}\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{(\log y - \mu_{LN})^2}{2\sigma_{LN}^2}}$; $g_E(y; \lambda_E) = \lambda_Ee^{-\lambda_Ey}$. Consider a mixture model that incorporates all three models: $g(y; \boldsymbol\theta) = p_Ng_N(y; (\mu_N, \sigma_N)) + p_{LN}g_{LN}(y; (\mu_{LN}, \sigma_{LN})) + (1 - p_N - p_{LN})g_E(y; \lambda_E)$, where $\boldsymbol\theta = (p_N, p_{LN}, \mu_N, \sigma_N, \mu_{LN}, \sigma_{LN}, \lambda_E)$. Figure 5.2.5 visualizes the ML estimate of this mixture model, which provides a markedly better approximation. [What is refuted] That for the displayed seven-parameter mixture, with the usual unrestricted parameter domain ($p_N, p_{LN} \ge 0$, $p_N + p_{LN} \le 1$, $\mu_N, \mu_{LN} \in \mathbb{R}$, $\sigma_N, \sigma_{LN}, \lambda_E > 0$), the sample likelihood has a maximizer. Theorem 5.2.6, with its regularity conditions, is not refuted, and the curve of Figure 5.2.5 is not shown to be numerically wrong. [Counterexample, from the validators] Take the sample $(y_1, y_2, y_3) = (1, 2, 3)$ and, for $\sigma > 0$, $\boldsymbol\theta_\sigma = (\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{4}, 1, \sigma, 0, 1, 1)$ (weights $\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{4}, \frac{1}{4}$). Then $g(1; \boldsymbol\theta_\sigma) \ge \frac{1}{2\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}$, $g(2; \boldsymbol\theta_\sigma) \ge \frac{e^{-2}}{4}$, $g(3; \boldsymbol\theta_\sigma) \ge \frac{e^{-3}}{4}$, so the likelihood satisfies $\prod_{i=1}^{3} g(y_i; \boldsymbol\theta_\sigma) \ge \frac{e^{-5}}{32\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}$, which exceeds any real bound $B$ at $\sigma = \frac{C}{|B| + 1}$ with $C = \frac{e^{-5}}{32\sqrt{2\pi}}$. Every admissible parameter vector has a finite likelihood at this sample, so no admissible vector maximizes the likelihood. In general, for any $n \ge 1$ and positive observations $y_1, ..., y_n$, with $\mu_N = y_1$, $\sigma_N = \sigma$ and the other parameters as above, $\prod_{i=1}^{n} g(y_i; \boldsymbol\theta) \ge \frac{e^{-\sum_{i=2}^{n} y_i}}{2 \cdot 4^{n-1}\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma} \to \infty$ as $\sigma \to 0$.

canonical_claim.note: Error rated Moderate (dual validation; confirmed in part). The first validator's artifact contains a Lean proof for the sample $(1, 2, 3)$ (runs/P001/validate/P001-C05-E002/v1/artifact/check.lean: full_likelihood_unbounded, no_full_global_maximum), with only the standard axioms. canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 5.2.5 and Example 5.2.11, corrected: maximization of the mixture likelihood qualified by existence of a maximum; the unrestricted mixture has unbounded likelihood on positive samples; a compact restriction under which a maximum is attained
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected passage] Then, as before, when $\prod_{i=1}^{n} g(Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i; \boldsymbol\theta)$ attains a finite maximum over the parameter space, its maximizer is the ML estimate of $\boldsymbol\theta$; the asymptotic properties of that estimate require the relevant regularity conditions (Theorem 5.2.6). For the unrestricted normal/log-normal/exponential mixture of Example 5.2.11 the sample likelihood is unbounded on positive samples, so a global ML estimate does not exist; Figure 5.2.5 shows a fitted mixture approximation (its objective and constraints are not documented). To retain a global sample-ML description, constraints or a penalty that prevent the collapse of a scale parameter must be specified and used. [Formal content] Let $g(y; \boldsymbol\theta)$ be the mixture density of Example 5.2.11 for $y > 0$. (i) For every $n \ge 1$ and all $y_1, ..., y_n > 0$: $\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta}\prod_{i=1}^{n} g(y_i; \boldsymbol\theta) = \infty$, the supremum being over $p_N, p_{LN} \ge 0$, $p_N + p_{LN} \le 1$, $\mu_N, \mu_{LN} \in \mathbb{R}$, $\sigma_N, \sigma_{LN}, \lambda_E > 0$; hence the likelihood has no maximizer. (ii) Let $B, S, b < \infty$ and $\delta, a > 0$, and restrict the parameters to the compact set $p_N, p_{LN} \ge 0$, $p_N + p_{LN} \le 1$, $|\mu_N|, |\mu_{LN}| \le B$, $\delta \le \sigma_N, \sigma_{LN} \le S$, $a \le \lambda_E \le b$. Assume the displayed restricted parameter set is nonempty. Then for all $y_1, ..., y_n > 0$ the likelihood $\boldsymbol\theta \mapsto \prod_{i=1}^{n} g(y_i; \boldsymbol\theta)$ is continuous on this set and attains its maximum there.
